subject: Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.

messages.author: 512996ea4ff0ea65
messages.subject: Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.
parts:
Hi Everybody


We are developing a framework for monitoring free roaming dog populations in the cities of Tierra del Fuego.

The objective is to monitor the mid and long term success of the policies to reduce free roaming dogs in the streets of the cities, like neuter and responsible pet ownership.

Cities are expanding in surface and adding new neigborhoods over the course of the years.

For that reason, and to avoid restrictions of design-based surveys, we are considering the use of Density Surface Models, also to be able to explain changes in dog presence by covariates.

Then, we should be able to tell the towns to follow a series of tracks (streets) that need to be surveyed over the years.

Adding covariates, we should be able to develop a DSM to assess abundance based on these covariates.



Then, here comest the two questions:

ONE:
The issue that comes to my mind and I want to share with you hast to do with modelling all over the space of the city, when free roaming dogs are distributed only along the streets.

The, the streets are like a mesh of something like 21m wide, separated by the about 800 blocks of around 90m side.

Potential solutions I was thinkg were:

1. Model the data as if they were collected and build a prediction grid where blocks can´t hold dogs (as if they are "0") meanwhile streets has a value of "1".

Then I wonder how much the smoothing all over the surface will affect the predicted results.

2. Model the data, but adding "dummy" transects located over some of the blocks, just to tell the model that inside the blocks   there are no dogs...

However the modelling may be affected  by the spatial spread of these dummy transects.....

3. Use something like the soap film smoother but I can´t figure out how we can handle such amount of  blocks... 



TWO:

About detectability of dogs.

When travelling along the streets we need to record  dogs that can walk freely at the sidewalks or at the streets. 

Streets has parked cars along the sidewalks, and many houses do not have fence, so dogs can sleep inside a parcel but leave the parcel boundarie as soon as they want to bark or whatever.

This impose visibility issues that affect detectability.

To reduce that I was thinking in make dogs more visible:
1. Survey the streets going behind garbage collectors, as these guys atract dogs either by their behavior (running along the streets) or leaving garbage behind ocasionally).
2. Broadcasting dog barks from the car meanwhile we go travelling.

I know that this affect the results of a survey, but if we want to see dogs in the streets I understand that we need to make them out


Any idea or previous experience in that is welcome. Many thanks

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.
parts:
Adrian:

I won't speak to all of the issues you raise in the investigation of feral dogs in urban environments.  One think I will point out is the challenge of credibly dealing with the assumption that animals are distributed independently of the transects.

The distribution of dogs in the vicinity (0-200m) perpendicular from the transect is not uniform.  Dogs know exactly where your transect is located and they are either attracted or repelled by the transect (as you note in discussion of garbage trucks).  You may see some dogs walking down the centre of the street, but many will be hugged against the walls of buildings that line the street; then occasionally you will be able to see hundred of metres down a crossing side street.

As you know, distance sampling is based around fitting detection functions to sightings.  To fit those functions, you assume that the only thing causing the number of sightings to diminish with distance from the transect is caused by distance (not by parked cars or mounds of trash or garbage trucks).  Consequently the use of distance sampling methods in urban settings is challenged.

If you can model the manner in which the dog gradient changes at small distances from the transect, then you might be able to produce both a model of the detection function and a model of the animal gradient.  See Marques et al. 2013 (http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10260-012-0223-2) for an example.  But as you can imagine the job is challenging.

parts:
Hi Eric.

Thanks for the comment, you are true.


I was thinking in modelling the counts of dogs along streets, using the street of each block as a "segment", to avoid issues related to dogs coming from crossing streets. 

Then I wonder if I can use "strip transect", taking the street width as the strip. At the end I should have a street traversed for let said 2 km, with something like 20 segments (depending on the length of the block), each segment with dog counts. How it looks?


Also, it cames now to my mind that going behind garbage trucks may attract dogs from crossing streets as well as dogs from the traversed streets. Would this be a problem if I want to have an index to assess yearly changes only abundance?

Adrian:

The proposition is becoming a bit stretched.  You describe that you want a 'strip transect' to be the width of the street.  Then model-based tools to predict animal density where we did not sample (off streets).  The model would make predictions to non-street (i.e. centres of city blocks), which I submit would be not a good idea.

Maybe it is simply late in the day and I have marked too many student papers today so my mood is not receptive to fresh ideas.  Perhaps other list members can be more supportive.

messages.author: 39f0839e8d6a4470
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Surveying free roaming dog populations in cities. Two questions.
parts:
Hi Adrian,

Interesting problem! I am a little further North in Chile in Valparaiso and we have plenty of street dogs here too. Some stray, many belonging to owners with no gardens so they just put a dog house / box on the street. I have heard that when the council came round to 'take action' all the dogs disappear off the streets!

I think you are more along the right idea with strip transects using the street width as the width of the strip. Is my understanding correct that you are only interested in the dogs on the streets? So your study region basically comprises of all the streets in the town?

If this is the case then you have 2 options, fit a model to the data ignoring the non-street areas, and then make predeictions about the density of dogs on all the streets. This should allow you to identify areas with higher densities of street dogs than others. The disadvantage of this is that some streets will be close together in space but in reality the dogs may actually need to travel quite a distance to get from one street to another. So a better approach might be to create your study region so that it only consists of the streets in the town then you could use this region to take into account the 'real' distances between points. For example, a method like CReSS http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10618600.2012.762920#.VHx-M4dJlXk 

I would say avoid garbage collection days. In my experience the dogs seems to form bigger pack on these days and travel further than they would normally. Sampling on garbage days I suspect would lead to lots of zero's and then a few very big counts, which is very bad for the modelling stage! On non-garbage days the dogs seem much more likely to stay local, I usually know which dogs I am likely to meet when I take a walk. I would say walking along the street, perhaps with a dog yourself, should draw out most dogs who can leave their properties.

What kinds of covariates were you plannng to put into the model? I guess you want to know if any of the techniques implemented are responsible for any changes, so including some measure of them. I also wonder if the level of provision for garbage collection factor. We have no communal bins locally, people just try to hang bags out of reach of the dogs, in comparison vina del mar seems to have a good system of communal bins.

Are you working on this with the Applied Ecology & Sustainability group at the Catholic University in Santiago? I hear they are looking at the stray dog population in Valdivia, although after a quick check they seem to be working in a more rural context.

Hope you find some of that useful,

Laura


 
Dr. L. Marshall

Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews
